content: The world is big and I want to have a good look at it before it gets dark.
In every walk with nature one receives far more than he seeks.
Heaven is under our feet as well as over our heads.
The Amazon rainforest is home to an estimated ten percent of all known species on Earth, making it one of the most biodiverse regions on the planet.
Coral reefs cover less than one percent of the ocean floor, yet they support roughly a quarter of all marine species.
Migratory birds can travel thousands of miles between breeding and wintering grounds, navigating using the sun, stars, and the Earth's magnetic field.
A single mature tree can absorb around twenty two kilograms of carbon dioxide per year, making forests an important part of regulating the planet's climate.
Bees pollinate roughly a third of the crops humans rely on for food, making them essential to global agriculture despite their small size.
The deepest part of the ocean, the Mariana Trench, plunges nearly eleven kilometers below the surface, deeper than Mount Everest is tall.
Deserts are defined by low precipitation rather than temperature, which is why some of the coldest places on Earth, including parts of Antarctica, are technically deserts.
Mycorrhizal fungi form partnerships with the roots of most plants, helping them absorb water and nutrients in exchange for sugars produced by photosynthesis.
Wolves live and hunt in structured packs, usually led by a breeding pair, and communicate through howls that can be heard for several kilometers.
The Sahara Desert was once a green landscape with lakes and grasslands, before a shift in the Earth's orbit altered rainfall patterns thousands of years ago.
Rivers shape the landscape around them over thousands of years, carving canyons and depositing sediment that forms fertile floodplains.
A rainforest canopy can be so dense that less than two percent of sunlight reaches the forest floor below.
